title: History of Nokia
wikitext:
{{Short description|History of the Finnish corporation}}
[[Nokia]] is a Finnish [[multinational corporation]] founded on 12 May 1865 as a single [[paper mill]] operation. Through the 19th century the company expanded, branching into several different products. In 1967, the Nokia corporation was formed. In the late 20th century, the company took advantage of the increasing popularity of computer and mobile phones. However, increased competition and other market forces caused changes in Nokia's business arrangements. In 2014, Nokia's mobile phone business was sold to Microsoft.

The name "Nokia" is derived from the town of [[Nokia, Finland]] and the nearby [[Nokianvirta]] River, which was located next to the company’s original factory. The commercial entities that preceded the modern-day Nokia company included ''Nokia Ab'' (Nokia company); ''Suomen Gummitehdas Oy'' (Finnish Rubber Works Ltd); and ''Suomen Kaapelitehdas Oy'' (Finnish Cable Works Ltd).<ref name="First-century">[http://company.nokia.com/en/about-us/our-company/our-story Our Story] Nokia Corporation 1 May 2014.</ref>

In 1865, the mining engineer, [[Fredrik Idestam]] established a [[Pulp mill|ground wood pulp mill]] on the banks of the [[Tammerkoski]] rapids in the town of [[Tampere]], in southwestern Finland. Tampere was then part of the [[Russian Empire]].<ref name="First-century" /> In 1868, Idestam built a second mill near the town of Nokia. Nokia lies {{convert|15|km|mi}} west of Tampere, by the Nokianvirta river. The river had better [[hydropower]] resources than those at Tampere.<ref name="Idestam">{{cite web|url=http://www.kansallisbiografia.fi/english/?id=4296|title=Idestam, Fredrik (1838–1916)|last=Helen|first=Tapio|publisher=Biographical Centre of the Finnish Literature Society|accessdate=22 March 2009}}</ref> In 1871, Idestam and [[Leo Mechelin]], a statesman and Idestam's friend, transformed Idestam's enterprises into a [[public limited company]] called ''Nokia Ab''.<ref name="Idestam"/>

In the late 1800s, Mechelin wanted to expand the company into the electricity business. However, Idestam refused. In 1896, Idestam retired and Mechelin became the company's chairman. He remained chairman from 1898 to 1914. During this time, Mechelin persuaded shareholders to allow the company to enter the electricity business.<ref name="Idestam"/> In 1902, Nokia commenced [[electricity generation]].<ref name="First-century" />

==20th century==
{{main article|Eduard Polón}}
[[File:Eduard Polon.png|thumb|Portrait of Eduard Polón by Eero Järnefelt.]]
[[Eduard Polón]] (1866 {{ndash}} 1930), was a Finnish business leader.<ref>Martin Häikiö ''Nokia Corporation 's official history'' Edita 2001, p.12 and 13.</ref> In 1898, Polón founded ''Suomen Gummitehdas Oy'' ([[Nokian Footwear|Finnish Rubber Works]]) - a manufacturer of [[galoshes]] and other rubber products.<ref name="First-century" /> In the early 1900s, the Finnish Rubber Works established factories near Nokia and used the town's name in the company's [[brand]]ing.<ref name="Nokian Footwear">{{cite web|url=http://nokianjalkineet.fi/en/our-story/|title=Nokian Footwear: Our Story|publisher=Nokian Footwear|accessdate=15 November 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129030031/http://nokianjalkineet.fi/en/our-story/|archive-date=29 November 2014}}</ref>

After [[World War I]], the Nokia Company was nearing bankruptcy and was acquired by the Finnish Rubber Works.<ref name="Kumi">{{cite book|last=Palo-oja|first=Ritva|author2=Willberg, Leena |title=Kumi – Kumin ja Suomen kumiteollisuuden historia|publisher=Tampere Museums|location=Tampere, Finland|year=1998|pages=43–53|isbn=9789516090651|language=fi}}</ref>

In 1932, the Finnish Rubber Works also acquired the ''Suomen Kaapelitehdas Oy'' ([[Kaapelitehdas|Finnish Cable Works]]). The cable works had been founded in 1912 by Arvid Wickström. His company produced [[Telephone cable|telephone]], [[Telegraphy|telegraph]], and [[electrical cables]].<ref name="First-century" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kaapelitehdas.fi/php/image.php?id=4856|title=Finnish Cable Factory – Brief History|format=PDF|publisher=kaapelitehdas.fi|accessdate=16 March 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070705233815/http://www.kaapelitehdas.fi/php/image.php?id=4856 |archive-date = 5 July 2007}}</ref>

In 1963, after 16 years as a technical director, [[Verner Weckman]] became the president of the Finnish Cable Works company. Weckman was a [[wrestler]] and was Finland's first [[Wrestling at the 1908 Summer Olympics – Men's Greco-Roman light heavyweight|Olympic Gold medallist]].<ref name="Weckman">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/verner-weckman |title=Nokia – Verner Weckman – Nokia's first century – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=20 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090225074458/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/verner-weckman |archive-date=February 25, 2009}}</ref> After [[World War II]], Finnish Cable Works supplied cables to the [[Soviet Union]] as part of its [[war reparations]]. This gave the company a foothold for later trade.<ref name="Weckman"/>

=== Nokia Corporation ===
[[File:Nokia capacitor.jpg|thumb|upright=0.5|A capacitor made by Nokia Capacitors]]

In 1967, Nokia Corporation was formed through the merger of the three companies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/the-merger |title=Nokia – The merger – Nokia's first century – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=16 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090223193956/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/the-merger |archive-date=February 23, 2009 }}</ref> The new company manufactured products including paper items, car and bicycle tires, [[Wellington boot|rubber boots]], communications cables, televisions and other consumer electronics, personal computers, generators, robotics,<ref>{{cite web|title=Industrial robot made by Nokia|url=https://fabryka-robotow.pl/2013/05/nokia-robotics/|website=Fabryka robotów|date=13 May 2013 |accessdate=7 February 2015|ref=nokia_robotics}}</ref> capacitors, [[Military technology and equipment]] (such as the [[Sanomalaite M/90|SANLA M/90]] device and the [[M61 gas mask]] for the [[Finnish Army]]), plastics, aluminum and chemicals.<ref name="Towards Telecommunications">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/NOKIA_COM_1/About_Nokia/Sidebars_new_concept/Broschures/TowardsTelecomms.pdf|title=Nokia – Towards Telecommunications|date=August 2000|publisher=Nokia Corporation|accessdate=5 June 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090710011202/http://www.nokia.com/NOKIA_COM_1/About_Nokia/Sidebars_new_concept/Broschures/TowardsTelecomms.pdf|archive-date=10 July 2009}}</ref><ref name="Cable electronics">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/first-electronic-dept |title=Nokia – First electronic dept – Nokia's first century – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=16 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090401232550/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/nokias-first-century/first-electronic-dept |archive-date=April 1, 2009 }}</ref>

In 1960, a cable division of the Nokia group had been formed. In 1962, it produced a [[pulse height analyzer]] used in [[nuclear power plant]]s.<ref name="Cable electronics"/> In 1967, an electronics division within the Nokia Corporation was formed. It operated for the next fifteen years, sometimes at a loss. Nokia researchers were encouraged to develop their own projects. This may have contributed to Nokia's focus on mobile phone technologies.<ref>{{cite book|last=Cord|first=David|title=[[The Decline and Fall of Nokia]]|date=April 2014|publisher=[[Schildts & Söderströms]]|isbn=978-951-52-3320-2|location=Helsinki|page=202}}</ref>

===Network equipment===
In the 1970s, Nokia produced the [[Nokia DX 200|Nokia DX 200]], a digital switch for telephone exchanges. The DX 200 became the workhorse of the network equipment division. Its architecture allowed it to be further developed into other switching products.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cs.helsinki.fi/u/kerola/tkhist/k2000/alustukset/puhelinkeskukset/|title=Automaattisten puhelinkeskusten historia|last=Kaituri|first=Tommi|year=2000|language=fi|accessdate=21 March 2009}}</ref> For example, in 1984, the development of an exchange for the [[Nordic Mobile Telephone]] network was begun.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.etla.fi/wp-content/uploads/2012/09/dp855.pdf|title=Overcoming a Technological Discontinuity – The Case of the Finnish Telecom Industry and the GSM|last=Palmberg|first=Christopher|author2=Martikainen, Olli |date=23 May 2003|publisher=The Research Institute of the Finnish Economy|accessdate=14 June 2009}}</ref> The network equipment division was merged with a Finnish State entity to form "Telefenno". In 1987, the state sold its shares in Telefenno to Nokia and in 1992, the name was changed to Nokia Telecommunications.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nokia : The Journey of a Company from Paper Pulp to Mobile Phones|url=https://news.biharprabha.com/2013/09/nokia-the-journey-of-a-company-from-paper-pulp-to-mobile-phones/|accessdate=4 September 2013}}</ref>

In 1998, the Israeli multinational company, [[Check Point]] which was founded in 1993, established a partnership with Nokia. Check Point's [[software]] was [[bundle (software distribution)|bundled]] with Nokia's [[network security]] tools.<ref name=Release3>{{cite web | url = http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Check+Point+Software+%26+Nokia+Expand+Partnership.-a056528104 | title = Check Point Software and Nokia Expand Partnership | publisher = Business Wire | date = 19 October 1999 | accessdate = 10 January 2013 | archive-date = 2 June 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130602162008/http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Check+Point+Software+%26+Nokia+Expand+Partnership.-a056528104 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

===Mobile radio telephony===
Prior to cellular mobile telephony, there was [[Mobile radio telephone|mobile radio telephony]]. In the 1960s, Nokia had started producing commercial and military mobile radio telephones. From 1964, Nokia had developed [[Very high frequency|VHF]] radios in collaboration with [[Salora Oy]]. From 1966, Nokia and Salora had developed [[Autoradiopuhelin|ARP]]s (''Autoradiopuhelin'' or radio car phones). In 1971, this technology became the first commercially available mobile phone network in Finland and in 1978, it offered 100 percent coverage in Finland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.it.lut.fi/kurssit/06-07/Ti5312600/luentokalvot/luento07-08.pdf|title=Siirtyvä tietoliikenne, luennot 7–8: Matkapuhelinverkot|last=Juutilainen|first=Matti|publisher=Lappeenranta University of Technology|language=fi|accessdate=22 March 2009|archive-date=26 March 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090326131656/http://www.it.lut.fi/kurssit/06-07/Ti5312600/luentokalvot/luento07-08.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the 1970s and 1980s, Nokia developed the ''Sanomalaitejärjestelmä'' (messaging system), a digital, portable and encrypted text-based communications device for the [[Finnish Defence Forces]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mil.fi/maavoimat/kalustoesittely/index.dsp?level=81|title=Puolustusvoimat: Kalustoesittely – Sanomalaitejärjestelmä|date=15 June 2005|publisher=The Finnish Defence Forces|language=fi|accessdate=14 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930205008/http://www.mil.fi/maavoimat/kalustoesittely/index.dsp?level=81|archive-date=30 September 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Nokia mobile telephone (1G) {{anchor|mobira}}===
[[File:Nokia 150 and nokia 1100.jpg|thumb|upright|The Mobira Cityman 150, Nokia's [[Nokia Mobile Telephone|NMT-900]] mobile phone from 1989 (left), compared to the [[Nokia 1100]], a GSM phone from 2003.<ref name="Nokia 1100">{{cite press release|title=Nokia 1100 phone offers reliable and affordable mobile communications for new growth markets |publisher=Nokia Corporation |date=27 August 2003 |url=http://press.nokia.com/PR/200308/915317_5.html |accessdate=26 May 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206070531/http://press.nokia.com/PR/200308/915317_5.html |archive-date=December 6, 2008 }}</ref><ref name="Mobira Cityman">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/mobira-cityman |title=Nokia – Mobira Cityman – The move to mobile – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226031732/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/mobira-cityman |archive-date=February 26, 2009 }}</ref>]]

In 1979, Nokia and Salora established a joint venture, "Mobira Oy".<ref name='ind_edgar'>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/analysis-and-features/microsoft-buys-nokia-150-year-history-of-finnish-company-with-humble-beginnings-8795907.html|date=3 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180703133445/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/analysis-and-features/microsoft-buys-nokia-150-year-history-of-finnish-company-with-humble-beginnings-8795907.html|archive-date=3 July 2018|access-date=1 June 2019|work=The Independent|author=James Edgar|title=Microsoft buys Nokia: 150-year history of Finnish company with humble beginnings|quote=Nokia created the radio telephone company Mobira Oy as a joint venture with Finnish television maker Salora in 1979}}</ref> Mobira developed mobile phones for the [[Nordic Mobile Telephone]] (NMT) network, called the "[[1G]]" and was the first fully automatic cellular phone system. It became commercially available in 1981.<ref name="Mobile era">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/mobile-era-begins |title=Nokia – Mobile era begins – The move to mobile – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=20 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226031727/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/mobile-era-begins |archive-date=February 26, 2009 }}</ref> In 1982, Mobira introduced its first [[car phone]], the "Mobira Senator" for NMT {{ndash}} 450 networks.<ref name="Mobile era"/>

In 1984, Nokia purchased Salora.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} Nokia's telecommunications division was renamed "Nokia-Mobira Oy". In the same year, the "Mobira Talkman", an early portable phone was launched. In 1987, Nokia introduced its first mobile phone, the "[[Mobira Cityman 900]]" for NMT{{ndash}} 900 networks. In comparison to the NMT {{ndash}} 450 network, there was a better signal strength but less coverage. While the Mobira Senator of 1982 had weighed {{convert|9.8|kg|abbr=on}} and the Talkman just under {{convert|5|kg|abbr=on}}, the Mobira Cityman weighed only {{convert|800|g|abbr=on}} including its battery. The phone, which was considered expensive, became an item indicating a high status.<ref name="Towards Telecommunications"/>

In 1987, the [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] leader [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] was seen using a Mobira Cityman in [[Helsinki]]. The phone developed the nickname, the "Gorba".<ref name="Mobira Cityman"/> In 1989, Nokia-Mobira Oy was renamed "Nokia Mobile Phones".

===Global system for mobile communications (2G)===
Nokia contributed to the development of the [[GSM]] [[2G]].<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://press.nokia.com/1997/10/17/nokia%C2%B4s-pioneering-gsm-research-and-development-to-be-awarded-by-eduard-rhein-foundation|title=Nokia's Pioneering GSM Research and Development to be Awarded by Eduard Rhein Foundation|date=17 October 1997|publisher=Nokia Corporation|accessdate=7 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120613185515/http://press.nokia.com/1997/10/17/nokia%C2%B4s-pioneering-gsm-research-and-development-to-be-awarded-by-eduard-rhein-foundation/|archive-date=13 June 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> It was able to carry [[data (computing)]] as well as voice traffic. [[Nordic Mobile Telephone|Nordic Mobile Telephony]] (NMT) was an early provider of international [[roaming]]. In 1987, GSM 2G became the new European standard for digital mobile technology.<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://gsmworld.com/newsroom/press-releases/2070.htm |title=Global Mobile Communication is 20 years old |date=6 September 2007 |publisher=GSM Association |accessdate=23 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090724194243/http://gsmworld.com/newsroom/press-releases/2070.htm |archive-date=July 24, 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.zdnet.co.uk/leader/0,1000002982,39289154,00.htm|title=Happy 20th birthday, GSM|date=7 September 2007|work=ZDNet.co.uk|publisher=CBS Interactive|accessdate=23 March 2009|archive-date=20 October 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081020002543/http://news.zdnet.co.uk/leader/0,1000002982,39289154,00.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1989, Nokia delivered its first GSM network to the Finnish operator [[Radiolinja]].<ref name="GSM">{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/first-gsm-call |title=Nokia – First GSM call – The move to mobile – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=20 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090330113453/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/the-move-to-mobile/first-gsm-call |archive-date=March 30, 2009 }}</ref> On 1 July 1991, in Helsinki, the first telephone call on the GSM G2 network was made by [[Harri Holkeri]], the [[Prime Minister of Finland]]. He used a [[prototype]] Nokia GSM phone to make the call.<ref name="GSM"/> In 1992, the first GSM phone, the [[Nokia 1011]], was made commercially available.<ref name="GSM"/><ref name="Nokia 1011">{{cite web|url=http://www.reghardware.co.uk/2007/11/09/ft_nokia_1011/|title=15 years ago: the first mass-produced GSM phone|last=Smith|first=Tony|date=9 November 2007|work=Register Hardware|publisher=Situation Publishing Ltd|accessdate=23 March 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120807122407/http://www.reghardware.com/2007/11/09/ft_nokia_1011/|archive-date=7 August 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> The model number, "1011" refers to its launch date on 10 November 1992.<ref name="Nokia 1011"/> In 1994, a branding [[ringtone]], the [[Nokia tune]], was included with the [[Nokia 2000 series|Nokia 2100 series]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/mobile-revolution/nokia-tune |title=Nokia – Nokia Tune – Mobile revolution – Story of Nokia |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=23 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090401231852/http://www.nokia.com/about-nokia/company/story-of-nokia/mobile-revolution/nokia-tune |archive-date=April 1, 2009 }}</ref>

The GSM 2G network and mobile phones provided improved voice calls, international roaming and support for new services such as [[text messaging]] ([[Short Message Service]] (SMS)).<ref name="GSM"/> In 2008, the GSM 2G network had approximately 3 billion users. There were at least 700 mobile phone commercial [[Mobile network operator|providers]] in 218 nations or territories. There were 15 mobile phone connections per second and 1.3 million mobile phone connections per day.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gsmworld.com/newsroom/press-releases/2008/1108.htm |title=3 Billion GSM Connections on the Mobile Planet – Reports The GSMA |date=16 April 2008 |publisher=GSM Association |accessdate=21 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081226095329/http://gsmworld.com/newsroom/press-releases/2008/1108.htm |archive-date=December 26, 2008 }}</ref>

===Personal computers===
[[File:Nokia booklet 3g-10 (3949263497).jpg|thumb|The [[Nokia Booklet 3G]] mini laptop.]]

In the 1980s, Nokia's computer division "Nokia Data" produced a series of personal computers called the "[[MikroMikko]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.old-computers.com/museum/computer.asp?st=1&c=630|title=Nokia MikroMikko 1|publisher=Old-Computers.com|accessdate=14 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430072629/http://www.old-computers.com/museum/computer.asp?st=1&c=630|archive-date=30 April 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref> It was aimed at the business market. MikroMikko 1, was released on 29 September 1981.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fujitsuservices.fi/historia/net/1980.htm|title=Net – Fujitsun asiakaslehti, Net-lehden historia: 1980-luku|publisher=Fujitsu Services Oy, Finland|language=fi|accessdate=22 March 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20110720183822/http://www.fujitsuservices.fi/historia/net/1980.htm|archive-date=20 July 2011}}</ref> Its competitor was the [[IBM personal computer]]. In 1991, Nokia Data was sold to a British company, [[International Computers Limited]] (ICL).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fujitsu.com/fi/about/history/1991/ |title=Historia: 1991–1999 |publisher=Fujitsu Services Oy, Finland |language=fi |accessdate=22 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008043049/http://www.fujitsu.com/fi/about/history/1991/ |archive-date=October 8, 2008 }}</ref>

Nokia produced [[Cathode ray tube]]s (CRT) and [[thin film transistor liquid crystal display]]s (|TFT LCDs) for personal computers and other applications. In 2000, Nokia sold its display products division to [[ViewSonic]].<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://press.nokia.com/PR/200001/775025_5.html |title=ViewSonic Corporation Acquires Nokia Display Products' Branded Business |date=17 January 2000 |publisher=Nokia Corporation |accessdate=22 March 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081209090630/http://press.nokia.com/PR/200001/775025_5.html |archive-date=December 9, 2008 }}</ref> However, in August 2009, Nokia released the [[Nokia Booklet 3G]] mini [[laptop]] which it continued for a short time.<ref name="Booklet 3G">{{cite press release|url=http://press.nokia.com/2009/08/24/nokia-booklet-3g-brings-all-day-mobility-to-the-pc-world/|title=Nokia Booklet 3G brings all day mobility to the PC world|date=24 August 2009|publisher=Nokia Corporation|accessdate=14 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106192601/http://press.nokia.com/2009/08/24/nokia-booklet-3g-brings-all-day-mobility-to-the-pc-world/|archive-date=6 January 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Other abandoned Nokia products include [[DSL modem]]s and digital [[set-top box]]es.

===Telecommunications===
In the 1980s under the chief executive officer (CEO) [[Kari Kairamo]], Nokia expanded, mostly through acquisitions. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, however, Nokia corporation experienced financial difficulties. Losses were made in the television manufacturing division.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.taloussanomat.fi/arkisto/2000/09/27/kari-kairamon-nousu-ja-tuho/200026243/12|title=Kari Kairamon nousu ja tuho|last=Pietilä|first=Antti-Pekka|date=27 September 2000|work=Taloussanomat|language=fi|accessdate=21 March 2009}}</ref> In 1988, [[Nokian Tyres]] became a separate entity.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nokiantyres.com/history-in-brief|title=History in brief|publisher=Nokian Tyres|accessdate=22 March 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090212122231/http://www.nokiantyres.com/history-in-brief|archive-date=12 February 2009}}</ref> Nokia's paper division was sold in 1989. In 1990, [[Nokian Footwear]] was a separate entity.<ref name="Nokian Footwear"/> During the rest of the 1990s, Nokia divested itself of all other businesses.<ref name="Jorma Ollila"/>
 
In 1988, Kairamo committed suicide. Following his death, [[Simo Vuorilehto]] became Nokia's chairman and CEO. From 1990 to 1993, Finland was in [[Early 1990s recession|recession]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cepr.org/PRESS/EP29%20finland.htm|title=Finland: How bad policies turned bad luck into a recession|publisher=Centre for Economic Policy Research|accessdate=5 April 2009|archive-date=14 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314112252/http://cepr.org/PRESS/EP29%20finland.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Vuorilehto made major changes to the Nokia corporation. The telecommunications division was stream-lined. The television and personal computing divisions were sold.<ref>{{cite book|last=Häikiö|first=Martti|others=Hackston, David (trans.)|title=Nokia Oyj:n historia 1–3 (A history of Nokia plc 1–3)|publisher=Edita|location=Helsinki|year=2001|isbn=951-37-3467-6|url=http://www.finlit.fi/booksfromfinland/bff/102/nokia.htm|accessdate=21 March 2008|language=fi|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071227000924/http://www.finlit.fi/booksfromfinland/bff/102/nokia.htm|archive-date=27 December 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1992, [[Jorma Ollila]] became CEO. He made telecommunications Nokia's sole concern.<ref name="Jorma Ollila"/> International sales increased relative to those in Finland.<ref name="Largest">{{cite At the end of the 2008 financial year, Nokia's smartphone market share had fallen to 40.8 percent from 50.9 percent a year earlier.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gartner.com/newsroom/id/910112 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130903165057/http://www.gartner.com/newsroom/id/910112 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 3, 2013 |title=Gartner Says Worldwide Smartphone Sales Reached Its Lowest Growth Rate With 3.7 Per Cent Increase in Fourth Quarter of 2008 |publisher=Gartner |date=11 March 2009 |accessdate=3 September 2013}}</ref> The [[Nokia E71]] became a success in the business market against competitors such as Apple and RIM.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Review: First Look: Nokia E71 faces off against iPhone 3G |url=https://www.itnews.com.au/feature/review-first-look-nokia-e71-faces-off-against-iphone-3g-408664 |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=iTnews}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Bray|first=Jonathan|url=http://www.trustedreviews.com/Nokia-E71_Mobile-Phone_review|title=Nokia E71 review|publisher=Trusted Reviews|date=5 February 2011|accessdate=3 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222051006/https://www.trustedreviews.com/Nokia-E71_Mobile-Phone_review|archive-date=2012-02-22|url-status=dead}}</ref> On 24 June 2008, Nokia bought the Symbian operating system and in 2009 made it [[open-source software|open source]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Ziegler |first=Chris |url=https://www.engadget.com/2008/06/24/nokia-buys-symbian/ |title=Nokia buys Symbian, turns software over to Symbian Foundation |work=Engadget |date=24 June 2008 |accessdate=3 September 2013}}</ref> The [[Nokia 5800 XpressMusic]] was the company's first major full-[[touchscreen]] device. It was a highly successful product, although in retrospect Nokia's decision to build a touch interface on top of S60 has been considered a mistake that led to its decline in the market by 2010.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peter |title=Flashback: Nokia 5800 XpressMusic - the little touchscreen that couldn't |url=https://www.gsmarena.com/flashback_the_story_of_the_nokia_5800_xpressmusic-news-38106.php |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=GSMArena.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In early 2009, Nokia released several devices such as the [[Nokia N97]], a touchscreen device with a landscape [[QWERTY]] slider keyboard that was focused on [[social networking]] which received mixed reviews and the [[Nokia E52]] which received positive reviews.<ref>{{cite web|last=Magennis|first=Niall|url=http://www.trustedreviews.com/Nokia-E52_Mobile-Phone_review|title=Nokia E52 review|publisher=Trusted Reviews|date=5 February 2011|accessdate=3 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140104001407/https://www.trustedreviews.com/Nokia-E52_Mobile-Phone_review|archive-date=2014-01-04|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Lewis |first=Frank |url=http://reviews.cnet.co.uk/mobile-phones/nokia-e52-review-49303566/ |title=Nokia E52 Review |publisher=CNET |date=7 September 2009 |accessdate=3 September 2013}}</ref> At the end of the 2008 financial year, Symbian's market share was 52.4 percent and at the same time in 2009, it was 46.1 percent with the loss going to Blackberry, iOS and Android.<ref>{{cite web|last=Schroeder |first=Stan |url=https://mashable.com/2010/02/23/gartner-smartphones/ |title=Smartphones in 2009: Symbian Dominates, iPhone, RIM and Android Rising Fast |publisher=Mashable |date=23 February 2010 |accessdate=3 September 2013}}</ref>

extract: Nokia is a Finnish multinational corporation founded on 12 May 1865 as a single paper mill operation. Through the 19th century the company expanded, branching into several different products. In 1967, the Nokia corporation was formed. In the late 20th century, the company took advantage of the increasing popularity of computer and mobile phones. However, increased competition and other market forces caused changes in Nokia's business arrangements. In 2014, Nokia's mobile phone business was sold to Microsoft.
